title: Denigrating a Peer Can Come Back to Haunt You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Warns leaders against the temptation to expose or smear a difficult peer, even when the peer hogs credit, backbites, or slacks. Using Lyndon Johnson's rule, never tell someone to go to hell unless you can send them there, the author argues that bad peers are rarely removed, so the attempt mostly creates an enemy. Word travels that you tried to smear them, and you may even end up reporting to them years later. Even when a peer stumbles and the moment to strike seems ripe, the advice is to resist and instead work around their dysfunction. The post concludes that the real casualty is your own credibility.
points: Johnson's maxim: do not attack someone unless you have the power to remove them, and in organizations you usually do not.
The usual outcome of exposing a bad peer is nothing, followed by word spreading that you smeared them.
The ironic risk is that years later the peer you attacked may become your boss.
When a peer finally stumbles, the author says not to strike; accept the situation and work around their dysfunction instead.
Denigrating a peer damages the denigrator's own credibility more than the target's.
quotes: Some peers hog credit, engage with others in passive-aggressive manner, don’t work very hard, or bad-mouth everyone else, including you. Given the opportunity, putting them in their place by exposing their bad behavior can be tempting. Waiting for the right moment to throw them under the bus sounds like a good idea but it is actually fraught with danger.

As a Senate leader, before he ascended to the Presidency, Johnson lived by a rule that is worth noting. As heavy-handed as he was with colleagues, he believed this: “Never tell someone to go to hell unless you can send them there.

In organizations, it is exceedingly difficult to send a bad peer to purgatory. You can denigrate their character with evidence or even convince others above you that they are harmful to the organization.
Word soon travels that you went out of your way to smear them. You now have an enemy that will use their negative traits against you at every chance they get.
If you can’t force them out of the organization, your best move is to accept the reality of the situation and work hard to circumvent their dysfunction. Anything else is foolhardy.
Denigrating a peer will almost always come back to haunt you. Instead of hurting them, you will more than likely derail your own credibility. Refrain from throwing any peer under the bus.
